title: Spotting numerical trouble in a log

questions.stem: You built a model with 1,240 nonzero coefficients. The first line of HiGHS's log says 1,238 nonzeros; there are no warnings and the status is OPTIMAL. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: Presolve removed two entries, as it always does before the search
options.says: The first line describes the model as received, before presolve.

options.text: Two coefficients were at or below 1e-9, and HiGHS treated them as zero
options.says: Right: entries at or below small_matrix_value, 1e-9 by default, are dropped without a warning.

options.text: Two coefficients were at or above 1e9, and HiGHS treated them as infinite
options.says: The 1e9 of the loan models reached HiGHS: its Matrix line printed it.

options.text: Two coefficients were near 1e-8, and HiGHS treated them as zero
options.says: A coefficient of 1e-8 was counted: dropped.py's first run shows 2 nonzeros.

origin.section: A Nonzero Count Lower Than You Built Means a Coefficient Was Dropped

questions.stem: A nightly MIP solve of a model with big-M rows ends with: Solution status feasible, 0 (bound viol.), 6.2e-07 (int. viol.), 0 (row viol.). HiGHS's integrality tolerance is 1e-6. What should the job do with the plan?

options.text: Accept it as is, since values below the tolerance count as exact
options.says: In lesson 10.1.1 an integrality violation of 8.89e-07, below the tolerance, was a free $889k loan.

options.text: Reject it, since a nonzero violation breaks a business rule
options.says: The plan is feasible within the tolerances; the line says where to look, not that a rule is broken.

options.text: Flag it, and check the binaries left between 0 and 1
options.says: Right: a nonzero integrality violation points at a binary between whole numbers; its coefficient says whether it matters.

options.text: Rerun with a 1e-9 tolerance, since that removes such plans
options.says: A tighter tolerance is a diagnosis, not a fix; the fix is to make the model's numbers fit the tolerance.

origin.section: The Report's Violation Lines Are the Solver's Audit of Its Own Plan

questions.stem: A model solved with a gap tolerance of 0 reports an optimum of $41,200k with presolve on and $41,950k with presolve off. Both runs end OPTIMAL. What does that tell you?

options.text: The model's numbers are suspect, since both runs should report one optimum
options.says: Right: presolve does not change which plans are allowed, so with a zero gap both runs must agree.

options.text: Presolve lost a better plan, since presolve may cut off allowed plans
options.says: Presolve removes nothing a plan needs; in the lessons the higher value was the wrong one.

options.text: Both values are right, since each optimum holds for its own settings
options.says: The settings do not change the model, so it has one optimum; one run is wrong.

options.text: The solver is broken, since a well-scaled model always gives one value
options.says: The trouble was in the models with M = 1e9; the tight model agreed four ways on the same solvers.

origin.section: Two Settings That Should Agree and Do Not Are a Numerical Symptom
